comments.text:
Great introduction,  except the false stories of Him who , the wrtoe that He killed his brother as a child and  the friend of The Great Khaan, Jamukha as His enemy. 
Enemies from a rival clan secretly shot and killed his younger brother, then made it appear as though Temüjin himself had killed him. They exploited a specific incident where the brothers had quarreled and the older brother had shot the younger one with a toy bow and arrow.
 Jamukha, His friend wasn't an enemy to Him, rather his great spy, actually. Even many of our Mongols still don't know about it..., believing how it was written in The Sercet History of The Mongols. 
Himself, The Great Khaan's spirit unraveled about this true story through a shaman, Tengerkhuu in the series of podcast called "From The Khaan to khaans", a few years ago.

replies.author: @WhereonEarth4K
replies.text: That's a fascinating alternate telling, and it's exactly the kind of detail that gets flattened when the popular version becomes "the" version. We'll take a closer look at the sourcing on that part.

comments.author: @leechumbley5440
comments.text: A most incredible story. The Mongols were undefeated in Europe, having made mincemeat of an army of German and Polish knights at Leignitz and all of Europe lay defenseless before them, when news came that the Great Khan had died and Batu gave the order to make haste back to Karakorum (he didn't get elected to Great Khan). Balkh, Kyiv, Baghdad with its House of Wisdom were all destroyed. I saw an exhibition where I learned they had a complicated and effective system of firing whistling arrows which were clear commands such that galloping warriors could suddenly change direction and no defenders had any answer to such speed, accuracy and flexibility. And yet, they had nothing to offer besides terror and dominance. It was the civilised who absorbed them, not the reverse. Having nothing to give themselves, the nomadic raiders eventually returned to their traditional way of life.

replies.author: @WhereonEarth4K
replies.text: That withdrawal after the Great Khan's death is one of history's great "what ifs" - Europe genuinely had no answer for that combination of speed and coordination, and yet you're right that conquest alone left nothing lasting behind. The whistling-arrow signaling system is a brilliant detail; that level of battlefield coordination centuries before radio is easy to underestimate. Thank you for such a rich addition.
